    Three flavours of conditional flow: base, coupling, both (and none)¶

    gauss_flows lets you make a flow conditional in three distinct places — the base distribution, the coupling layers, or both — with one consistent API: a single condition keyword that threads through SurVAEFlow.log_prob(...) and SurVAEFlow.sample(...). This notebook walks through the math of each variant, then shows the four resulting fits side by side on the two-moons dataset from notebook 01 (gaussianization_flow_2d).

    We use the class label that notebook 01 discards (_, y = make_moons(...)) as the conditional context $c$. make_moons returns $y \in \{0, 1\}$ indicating which crescent each point belongs to, so $p(x \mid y=0)$ is the upper moon and $p(x \mid y=1)$ is the lower moon — two well-separated, single-crescent conditional densities, well within RQSplineCoupling capacity.

    0. Math primer — conditional normalizing flows¶

    A normalizing flow defines a density on $x \in \mathbb{R}^D$ via an invertible map $f_\theta : \mathbb{R}^D \to \mathbb{R}^D$ pulling samples back to a tractable base distribution $p_Z$:

    $$ p_X(x) \;=\; p_Z\!\big(f_\theta(x)\big) \,\left| \det \frac{\partial f_\theta}{\partial x}(x) \right|. $$

    For a chain $f_\theta = f_K \circ \cdots \circ f_1$ with intermediate states $z_k = f_k(z_{k-1})$, $z_0 = x$:

    $$ \log p_X(x) \;=\; \log p_Z(z_K) \;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{K} \log\!\left| \det \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial z_{k-1}}(z_{k-1}) \right|. $$

    To make this conditional on a context $c \in \mathbb{R}^{D_c}$, any of the three pieces — the base $p_Z$, the maps $f_k$, or both — can be made functions of $c$. The general conditional flow density is

    $$ p_X(x \mid c) \;=\; p_Z\!\big(f_\theta(x; c) \,\big|\, c\big) \,\left| \det \frac{\partial f_\theta(\cdot\,;c)}{\partial x}(x) \right|. $$

    The four variants in this notebook correspond to which factors are functions of $c$:

    | Variant | Density | |---|---| | None | $p_X(x) = p_Z\!\big(f_\theta(x)\big)\,\big|\det J_{f_\theta}(x)\big|$ | | Base only | $p_X(x \mid c) = p_Z\!\big(f_\theta(x) \,\big|\, c\big)\,\big|\det J_{f_\theta}(x)\big|$ | | Coupling only | $p_X(x \mid c) = p_Z\!\big(f_\theta(x; c)\big)\,\big|\det J_{f_\theta(\cdot;c)}(x)\big|$ | | Both | $p_X(x \mid c) = p_Z\!\big(f_\theta(x; c) \,\big|\, c\big)\,\big|\det J_{f_\theta(\cdot;c)}(x)\big|$ |

    Conditional base — ConditionalDiagGaussian¶

    A diagonal Gaussian whose location and log-scale are functions of $c$:

    $$ p_Z(z \mid c) \;=\; \prod_{d=1}^{D} \mathcal{N}\!\big(z_d \,\big|\, \mu_d(c),\, \sigma_d(c)^2\big), \qquad [\mu(c),\, \log \sigma(c)] \;=\; g_\phi(c), $$

    where $g_\phi$ is a small MLP. Closed-form log-density:

    $$ \log p_Z(z \mid c) \;=\; -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{d=1}^{D}\left[ \frac{(z_d - \mu_d(c))^2}{\sigma_d(c)^2} \;+\; \log\!\big(2\pi\,\sigma_d(c)^2\big) \right]. $$

    This handles per-class shifts: if the only thing that varies with $c$ is the position of the mode, the conditional base alone is enough.

    Conditional coupling — RQSplineCoupling(cond_dim=...)¶

    A coupling layer splits $x = (x_a, x_b)$ on a binary mask. The "passthrough" half $x_a$ is left alone; the "active" half $x_b$ goes through an elementwise transformer $\tau$ whose parameters are produced by a conditioner MLP $h_\psi$ that already takes $x_a$ as input. Adding cond_dim > 0 simply concatenates the external context $c$ to that input:

    $$ \begin{aligned} y_a &= x_a, \\ y_b &= \tau\!\big(x_b;\, \theta\big), \qquad \theta = h_\psi\!\big([x_a, c]\big). \end{aligned} $$

    For an RQSplineCoupling, $\tau(\cdot;\theta)$ is a rational-quadratic spline whose knot positions and slopes come from $\theta$. The Jacobian is triangular by construction, so

    $$ \log\!\left| \det \frac{\partial (y_a, y_b)}{\partial (x_a, x_b)} \right| \;=\; \sum_{i \in \text{active}} \log \tau'\!\big(x_{b,i};\, \theta_i\big). $$

    This handles per-class shape warps: the spline knots can move with $c$, producing genuinely class-specific maps.

    How the package routes condition¶

    Each layer (and the base) declares whether it is conditional via a static attribute cond_shape:

    • cond_shape is None → unconditional layer; the layer ignores any condition argument it receives.
    • cond_shape == (D_c,) → conditional layer; it expects a context of that shape.

    SurVAEFlow.log_prob(x, key, condition=c) (and .sample(key, condition=c)) takes a single c and broadcasts it to every opted-in layer. There is no per-layer condition kwarg — you build the chain, decide for each layer whether it should look at $c$ via cond_dim=..., and the same $c$ flows through. flowjax's _check_condition decorator raises if you forget to pass a context to a conditional layer.

    For class-conditional density estimation specifically, ClassCondFlow(n_classes=..., event_shape=..., transforms=[...]) is sugar for "conditional base + unconditional transforms" with a label kwarg in place of condition. We don't use it here because we want to expose all four variants explicitly.

    For transforms that genuinely cannot take a context (rotations, normalizations, etc.), wrap them in Conditioner(inner=..., cond_shape=(D_c,), context_net=g_\phi) to add a FiLM-style affine modulation around the inner transform:

    $$ y \;=\; \exp\!\big(\log s(c)\big) \cdot f_{\text{inner}}(x) \;+\; t(c), \qquad [t(c), \log s(c)] = g_\phi(c). $$

    1. Configurations under test¶

    We compare four configurations under identical hyperparameters:

    1. None (baseline = notebook 01's setup): a fixed $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$ base + unconditional RQSplineCoupling chain. The flow ignores $y$ entirely and fits the marginal — the full two-moons. Useful as a sanity check; reproduces notebook 01's fit quality.
    2. Base only: a ConditionalDiagGaussian base whose $\mu, \log \sigma$ come from the one-hot $y$, paired with the same unconditional RQSplineCoupling chain. The base shifts per class but the chain learns one shared crescent shape.
    3. Coupling only: a fixed $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$ base, paired with RQSplineCoupling(cond_dim=2) layers that read the one-hot $y$. The couplings learn class-specific shapes; class-specific shift has to be absorbed through the spline parameters — awkward, but doable for two-moons.
    4. Both: conditional base and conditional couplings — the same one-hot label flows to both. Full capacity.

def style_axes(ax, *, aspect=None, grid=True):
    if grid:
        ax.minorticks_on()
        ax.grid(True, which="major", linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.6)
        ax.grid(True, which="minor", linewidth=0.4, alpha=0.3)
    if aspect is not None:
        ax.set_aspect(aspect)
    return ax


def style_jointgrid(g, aspect="equal"):
    style_axes(g.ax_joint, aspect=aspect)
    style_axes(g.ax_marg_x, grid=False)
    style_axes(g.ax_marg_y, grid=False)
    for spine in ("top", "right"):
        g.ax_marg_x.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
        g.ax_marg_y.spines[spine].set_visible(False)

    3. Four flow configurations¶

    Each flow uses the same chain of four RQSplineCoupling layers separated by fixed permutations — splines for capacity, since fitting two-moons is not affine. The only difference between the four configurations is where conditioning happens.

    Flow Base $p_Z$ Couplings $f_\theta$ What can it model?
    flow_none $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$ unconditional only the marginal $p(x)$ — ignores $y$
    flow_base $\mathcal{N}(\mu(c), \sigma(c)^2 I)$ unconditional per-class shift only
    flow_coupling $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$ cond_dim=2 per-class shape warps
    flow_both $\mathcal{N}(\mu(c), \sigma(c)^2 I)$ cond_dim=2 both — full capacity

    Architectural detail. A coupling layer leaves half the dims untouched, so we interleave fixed Permute layers between couplings to ensure every dim gets transformed. With $D=2$ and a 1-vs-1 split, a single Permute([1, 0]) between couplings is enough. We use spline transformers (rational-quadratic, 8 bins, interval $[-4, 4]$) because affine couplings cannot bend a Gaussian into a crescent.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    N_LAYERS = 4
EVENT = (2,)
COND_DIM = 2  # one-hot (2,)


def make_flow(*, base_cond: bool, coupling_cond: bool, key):
    """Build an N_LAYERS-layer SurVAEFlow with the requested conditioning."""
    base_key, *layer_keys, perm_key = jr.split(key, N_LAYERS + 2)
    if base_cond:
        base = ConditionalDiagGaussian(
            base_key, event_shape=EVENT, cond_shape=(COND_DIM,)
        )
    else:
        base = Normal(jnp.zeros(EVENT))
    cond_dim = COND_DIM if coupling_cond else None
    perm = jr.permutation(perm_key, jnp.arange(EVENT[0]))
    transforms = []
    for i, k in enumerate(layer_keys):
        transforms.append(
            RQSplineCoupling(
                k,
                shape=EVENT,
                n_bins=8,
                interval=4.0,
                cond_dim=cond_dim,
                nn_width=64,
                nn_depth=2,
            )
        )
        if i < N_LAYERS - 1:
            transforms.append(Permute(perm))
    return SurVAEFlow(base, transforms)


CONFIGS = [
    ("none", dict(base_cond=False, coupling_cond=False)),
    ("base only", dict(base_cond=True, coupling_cond=False)),
    ("coupling only", dict(base_cond=False, coupling_cond=True)),
    ("both", dict(base_cond=True, coupling_cond=True)),
]
flows = {
    name: make_flow(**kw, key=jr.key(11 + i)) for i, (name, kw) in enumerate(CONFIGS)
}
for name, flow in flows.items():
    n_params = sum(
        int(np.prod(p.shape))
        for p in jax.tree_util.tree_leaves(eqx.filter(flow, eqx.is_array))
    )
    print(f"{name:>14s}  trainable params: {n_params:6d}")

    4. Train each flow¶

    All four flows minimize the same objective — negative log-likelihood under the model:

    $$ \mathcal{L}(\theta, \phi) \;=\; -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x, c) \sim \mathcal{D}}\big[\log p_X(x \mid c)\big] \;=\; -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x, c)}\!\left[\log p_Z(z_K \mid c) + \sum_{k=1}^K \log \big| \det J_{f_k}(z_{k-1}; c) \big|\right] $$

    with $z_K = f_\theta(x; c)$. For the "none" and "coupling only" variants the $\,\cdot\, \mid c\,$ on the base drops out; for the "none" and "base only" variants the $c$ inside $f_k$ drops out. Same code path for all four — only the layers' cond_shapes differ.

    We wrap SurVAEFlow as a flowjax.distributions.AbstractDistribution so fit_to_data can auto-vmap over the batch. Hyperparameters match notebook 01 (learning_rate=5e-3, batch_size=256, max_epochs=600, max_patience=30).

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    class SurVAEFlowAdapter(AbstractDistribution):
    """Adapt a bijection-only SurVAEFlow to flowjax's AbstractDistribution API.

    SurVAEFlow.log_prob has signature (x, key, condition); flowjax expects
    (x, condition) and auto-vmaps over batched x and condition. The key in
    SurVAEFlow's signature is consumed by stochastic surjections only; for
    a bijection-only chain it is unused, so we fix it deterministically.
    """

    flow: SurVAEFlow
    shape: tuple[int, ...]
    cond_shape: tuple[int, ...] | None

    def __init__(self, flow):
        self.flow = flow
        self.shape = flow.data_shape
        # Always declare cond_shape so the adapter accepts a context. The
        # "none" flow internally ignores it (no opted-in layers).
        self.cond_shape = (COND_DIM,)

    def _log_prob(self, x, condition=None):
        return self.flow.log_prob(x, jr.key(0), condition=condition)

    def _sample(self, key, condition=None):
        return self.flow.sample(key, condition=condition)


def train(flow, *, key):
    adapter = SurVAEFlowAdapter(flow)
    trained, losses = fit_to_data(
        key,
        adapter,
        (X, C),
        learning_rate=5e-3,
        max_epochs=600,
        max_patience=30,
        batch_size=256,
        val_prop=0.1,
        show_progress=False,
    )
    return trained.flow, losses


trained = {}
losses_all = {}
for name, _ in CONFIGS:
    print(f"training: {name}")
    trained[name], losses_all[name] = train(
        flows[name], key=jr.key(20 + abs(hash(name)) % 1000)
    )

    5. Per-class sample comparison¶

    To draw conditional samples we exploit invertibility:

    $$ z \sim p_Z(\cdot \mid c), \qquad x \;=\; f_\theta^{-1}(z;\, c). $$

    For each variant we draw $N$ samples per class and overlay them on the true class samples. Two rows (one per class) × four columns (one per configuration). The "none" flow has no class information — its panel is the same in both rows by construction.

        [1.0, 0.0],  # y = 0  → upper moon

    dtype=jnp.float32,

class_labels_text = ["y = 0 (upper moon)", "y = 1 (lower moon)"]

n_per_panel = 2000


def true_class_samples(class_idx):
    mask = y == class_idx
    return X[mask][:n_per_panel]


def flow_samples(flow, n, c, *, key):
    cond = jnp.broadcast_to(c, (n, COND_DIM))
    keys = jr.split(key, n)
    return jax.vmap(lambda k, ci: flow.sample(k, condition=ci))(keys, cond)

    What to look for

    • None (column 1): the flow ignores $y$ — it samples from the full two-moons every time, so half the samples land in the wrong crescent. The light blue (true class) and orange (flow) only partially overlap.
    • Base only (column 2): the per-class mean is correct, but the unconditional spline chain learned one shape that has to serve both classes — the per-class crescent shape is muddier than the truth.
    • Coupling only (column 3): the spline couplings can read the one-hot label and produce class-specific crescents. Position and shape both come out cleanly because the couplings have enough capacity to absorb the per-class shift through the spline parameters.
    • Both (column 4): same crisp per-class fit as coupling-only, with the conditional base providing a per-class warm-start. The end-game NLL is the lowest.

    6. Quantitative comparison¶

    Mean per-example conditional log-likelihood under each fitted model:

    $$ \widehat{\mathcal{L}\!\!L}(\theta, \phi) \;=\; \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N \log p_X(x_n \mid c_n). $$

    Computed on the training set — we have no held-out oracle, but the four configurations can still be ranked.

    7. Takeaways¶

    Modelling guidance.

    • Pick what to condition based on what your data needs. If only the position of $p(x \mid c)$ varies with $c$ (location shift, isotropic scale), a conditional base alone is enough. If the shape varies — as it does here, since each class is a different crescent rather than a translated copy — conditional couplings are the natural fit. Real datasets usually benefit from both.
    • The conditioning capacity is multiplicative across layers. With $K$ conditional couplings, the per-class map composes $K$ class-dependent splines. A single conditional base contributes one Gaussian. Stacking helps mostly when the conditional density family is genuinely complex.
    • Keep $D_c$ modest. The conditioner MLPs concatenate $c$ to $x_a$, so $D_c$ inflates the input layer. For categorical $y$ with many classes, prefer a learned embedding $e(y) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ over one-hot encoding.

    Implementation guidance for gauss_flows.

    • The same condition keyword threads everywhere. SurVAEFlow.log_prob(x, key, condition=c) and .sample(key, condition=c) broadcast $c$ to every layer that opted in (cond_shape is not None); other layers ignore it. There is no per-layer condition kwarg.
    • Inside a coupling there are two streams. The untransformed half of $x$ is always a conditioning input — that is how coupling layers work. Adding cond_dim > 0 also concatenates the external context onto the inner MLP. The two streams are merged inside flowjax and you never slice them apart from outside.
    • For class-conditional density estimation, prefer ClassCondFlow(n_classes=..., event_shape=..., transforms=[...]). It pairs a ClassCondDiagGaussian base (per-class learnable $\mu, \log \sigma$) with an arbitrary chain of unconditional transforms, exposing a label keyword in place of condition. The construction validates that no transform in the chain is conditional, since the label flows only to the base.
    • For transforms that genuinely cannot take a context (rotations, normalizations, periodic shifts), wrap them in Conditioner(inner=..., cond_shape=(D_c,), context_net=g_\phi). The wrapper applies a FiLM-style affine modulation $\,y = \exp(\log s(c)) \cdot f_{\text{inner}}(x) + t(c)\,$ around the inner transform — preserving invertibility and giving a closed-form log-determinant — and rejects inner transforms that are already conditional.
    • Errors fail fast. Forgetting to pass condition to a flow with any conditional layer raises in flowjax's _check_condition decorator; passing a wrong-shape context fails the same way.
